title: When Heaven Is About to Confer a Great Task
author: Mingde
excerpt: [Hardship and distress carve you into perfection, as jade] The tempering of hardship and distress is like carving jade into a vessel — it brings you to success.

inline.s: Selected from Mencius, “Gaozi, Part Two”
Hardship and distress carve you into perfection, as jade.
[Hardship and distress carve you into perfection, as jade] The tempering of hardship and distress is like carving jade into a vessel — it brings you to success.
[Shun rose from the furrows
quǎn
of the fields; Fu Yue
yuè
was raised from his toil at walls and ramparts; Jiao Ge
gé
was raised from fish and salt; Guan Yiwu was raised from the prison officer’s hands; Sun Shu’ao was raised from the seashore; and Baili Xi was raised from the marketplace.]

Shun was discovered and raised up while plowing the fields; Fu Yue was raised up while laboring at the building of walls; Jiao Ge was raised up while fishing and drying salt; Guan Zhong was raised up from among captives and prisoners; Sun Shu’ao was raised up from a remote seashore; and Baili Xi was bought back from the slave market and raised up.
[Shun] Surnamed Yao and named Chonghua. In the time of Emperor Yao he plowed at Mount Li; Emperor Yao passed the throne of the Son of Heaven to him.
[Furrows (
quǎn
)] fields; the open country.
[Fu Yue (
yuè

)] In the Shang dynasty he was a convict laborer, building walls at Fuxian. King Wuding of Shang wished to revive the kingdom, and sent men to seek him in the wilds; they found Fu Yue, and the king raised him to be prime minister, and the kingdom was greatly well-governed.
[Rammed-earth walls] In ancient times walls were built by pouring earth between two boards and pounding it firm with a pestle. Zhù is the pestle used to pound the earth. [Jiao Ge (
gé
)] A high minister of King Zhou of Shang, counted among the worthies together with Weizi, Jizi, and Prince Bigan.

[Guan Zhong] Surnamed Guan, named Yiwu, courtesy name Zhong, a statesman of the state of Qi in the early Spring and Autumn period. After Duke Huan of Qi came to the throne, he was recommended by Bao Shuya and appointed prime minister, enabling Duke Huan to achieve hegemony. [Shì] a prison officer. [Sun Shu’ao] In the Spring and Autumn period he was the lingyin (prime minister) of the state of Chu. [Baili Xi] He was bought back from the slave market by Duke Mu of Qin with five ram skins and entrusted with government, enabling Qin to “open up a thousand li of land and become hegemon of the western Rong,” making it one of the “Five Hegemons of the Spring and Autumn period.”

[Therefore, when Heaven is about to confer a great task on such a man, it will first bitter his heart and will, weary his sinews and bones, starve his body and flesh, plunge him into poverty and want, and confound and thwart all that he does. In this way it stirs his mind, steels his nature, and adds
(same as “increase”)
to what he is unable to do.]

Thus, when Heaven is about to send a great mission down upon such a person, it will first afflict his heart and will, weary his sinews and bones, starve and chill his body, make him suffer every want and peril, confound all that he does, and bring him repeated setbacks. Through these it tempers and polishes his mind to lift it higher, makes his character resolute, courageous, and unyielding, and adds to the abilities and inner qualities he originally lacked.
Hardship and distress, setbacks and failures, are the forging of iron into steel, the adding to what one is unable to do. Therefore do not be afraid, and still less let any challenge go to waste!

[Forging iron into steel] Here “forging” means hammering at high temperature. Through repeated high-temperature forging, the impurities in the iron blank are removed, the carbon content is lowered, and its metallurgical structure is improved, until it becomes a fine steel implement — this is what is meant by “a hundred forgings make steel.” The treasured sword that slices iron like mud and severs a hair blown against its edge is made by just such a thousand hammerings and forgings.

[A man must often err, and only then can he correct himself. His mind must be distressed and his thoughts tangled, and only then does he rise to action. Only when these are shown in his countenance and voiced in his words do others come to understand him.]

A person must always pass through countless setbacks and failures before he can be reborn into a new self (a carp turning into a dragon). His mind must be distressed and imperiled, and he must ponder and deliberate repeatedly, and only then can he accomplish something. Only when his lofty ambitions and great talents for governing the age flow forth naturally and are voiced in his words can he be understood by others.

[A man must often err, and only then can he correct himself] A person must always pass through countless setbacks and failures before he can be reborn into a new self. [A carp turning into a dragon] An ancient legend says that when a Yellow River carp leaps over the Dragon Gate, it transforms into a dragon. [Distressed and imperiled] hard-pressed and in danger. [Thoughts tangled] pondering and deliberating repeatedly. [Understand] to make others understand.
[If within the state there are no law-abiding ministers and no assisting
bì
officials, and without there are no hostile states or external calamities, the state will invariably perish.]

A state that within has no law-abiding ministers and worthy officials to assist it with distressed minds and tangled deliberations, and without has no threat from hostile states or external calamities that could break its houses and destroy the realm, will surely perish.
[Law-abiding ministers] ministers who strictly uphold the law.
[Assisting (
bì
) officials] worthy officials who aid the ruler. Fú here is the same as bì , to assist.
[Then one understands: through adversity and peril there is life, and through ease and pleasure there is death.]
Thus one knows: anxiety and peril enable a person, and even a state, to survive and develop, while idle ease and pleasure cause a person, and even a state, to decay and perish.
